name: Ottawa
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Ottawa: federal procurement partners, technology diligence, lobbying exposure and Ontario-Quebec records.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Ottawa, scoped from Nashville: research on federal contractors and their partners, diligence on Kanata technology and defence firms, government relations exposure, and factual support for counsel in disputes before Ontario and federal courts in Canada's capital.
intro: Ottawa is Canada's capital and, with Gatineau across the river in Quebec, forms a census metropolitan area that Statistics Canada estimated at 1,660,269 people on 1 July 2024. The federal government is the region's defining employer: the City of Ottawa reports that public administration and health and education each account for about a fifth of employment, and the region hosts dozens of federal research laboratories. Ottawa also has a deep technology sector, centred on Kanata, with the City describing the highest concentration of tech talent in Canada. Telecommunications, software, cybersecurity, defence electronics and professional services firms cluster around federal customers and research institutions.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Ottawa because so much of it touches the federal state. Companies bidding for or delivering federal contracts want to understand the ownership, history and integrity record of partners, subcontractors and consultants. Investors and acquirers in Ottawa technology and defence firms need background on founders, executives and foreign relationships, particularly where government contracts or sensitive technology are involved. Government relations activity raises questions about who is advising whom. And because the metropolitan area spans Ontario and Quebec, a single matter can require research under two provincial legal systems with different languages, registries and privacy rules.

matters.title: Federal contract partner due diligence
matters.text: Background research on joint-venture partners, subcontractors and consultants in federal procurements, covering ownership, management, related companies, litigation, regulatory history and media coverage, so bidders and prime contractors can assess integrity and conflict-of-interest risks before teaming agreements are signed.

matters.title: Technology and defence investment diligence
matters.text: Research on Ottawa technology, cybersecurity and defence electronics companies and their principals ahead of investment or acquisition, including corporate history, prior ventures and insolvencies, litigation, intellectual property disputes and publicly reported foreign relationships that may matter to investors or government customers.

matters.title: Government relations and lobbying exposure
matters.text: Reviewing publicly available lobbying registrations, political contribution records and media to understand which consultants and former officials advise a counterparty, helping clients identify reputational or conflict-of-interest issues before relying on a government relations adviser or entering a partnership.

matters.title: Cross-river Ontario and Quebec research
matters.text: Assembling records across both sides of the Ottawa River, where a company or individual may be registered, own property or litigate in Quebec while operating in Ontario, and where French-language Quebec records and different civil law concepts must be read alongside Ontario sources.

matters.title: Internal investigations in technology firms
matters.text: Support to counsel investigating suspected misconduct such as departing employees taking confidential information, vendor kickbacks or misrepresented credentials, focused on lawful background research into the people and companies involved and on presenting findings that counsel can test.

local_context.title: Federal and Ontario courts
local_context.text: Ottawa is the seat of the Supreme Court of Canada and the principal seat of the Federal Court and Federal Court of Appeal, which hear matters such as intellectual property, federal administrative decisions and claims against the Crown. Ordinary commercial disputes in the city go to the Ontario Superior Court of Justice sitting in Ottawa, with appeals to the Court of Appeal for Ontario. Filings in these courts are a primary source on local counterparties.

local_context.title: Ontario investigator licensing
local_context.text: Ontario's Private Security and Investigative Services Act, 2005 requires anyone who acts as or holds themselves out as a private investigator to hold a licence and to work for a licensed or registered entity. A Registrar of Private Investigators and Security Guards administers the regime. Lawyers practising their profession, peace officers and certain insurance and credit reporting activities are exempt, as are out-of-province licensed investigators entering solely for a cross-border investigation.

local_context.title: Gatineau and Quebec rules
local_context.text: Gatineau, part of the same metropolitan area, sits in Quebec, where private law follows the Civil Code of Quebec, businesses register with the Registraire des entreprises and private-sector privacy is governed by Quebec's own legislation. Quebec also has its own investigator licensing. A matter involving employees, property or companies on the Quebec side therefore needs separate legal review, French-language research and, where field work is needed, Quebec-licensed professionals.

local_context.title: Federal integrity and lobbying records
local_context.text: Because so many Ottawa businesses depend on federal customers, federal oversight records are useful context. Lobbying activity directed at federal institutions is publicly registered with the Commissioner of Lobbying, and federal procurement is subject to integrity and ineligibility rules administered by Public Services and Procurement Canada. These sources do not establish wrongdoing on their own but help map relationships around a counterparty.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Ottawa, TDSC first determines which governments' rules apply: federal, Ontario, Quebec, or more than one. Desk research is then conducted from Nashville using Corporations Canada and provincial business registries, Ontario, Quebec and federal court records, public lobbying and procurement information, and English and French-language media. Because Ontario requires private investigators to be licensed under the Private Security and Investigative Services Act, 2005, and Quebec has its own regime, any interviews, surveillance or field enquiries are carried out by appropriately licensed local professionals coordinated with the client's Canadian counsel. Personal information is handled in line with federal and, where relevant, Quebec privacy law, and findings are reported with sources.

faqs.q: Can you vet a teaming partner for a Canadian federal contract?
faqs.a: Yes. We research the partner's corporate history, directors, related entities, litigation, regulatory and procurement-related public records, lobbying registrations and media coverage. We do not access security clearance or other restricted government information. Whether a partner is eligible under federal procurement rules is a question for the client's counsel and the contracting authority.

faqs.q: Do you need an Ontario licence to work on matters in Ottawa?
faqs.a: Ontario requires people acting as private investigators in the province to be licensed under the Private Security and Investigative Services Act, 2005. TDSC does not hold an Ontario licence. Desk research is performed from Nashville; any field enquiries, interviews or surveillance in Ottawa are carried out by licensed Ontario investigators whom we coordinate with counsel.

faqs.q: Our matter involves people in Gatineau as well as Ottawa. Does that change anything?
faqs.a: Yes. Gatineau is in Quebec, which has its own civil law, business registry, privacy legislation and investigator licensing. We research Quebec records in French alongside Ontario sources and ensure any field work on the Quebec side is done by Quebec-licensed professionals. Counsel should confirm which province's law governs each step.

faqs.q: Can you look into an Ottawa technology company's foreign connections?
faqs.a: We can research publicly available information on shareholders, directors, financing announcements, partnerships, litigation and media coverage, including foreign-language sources where relevant, and identify related companies abroad. We report what is documented and what is inferred. National security reviews and export controls are matters for counsel and the relevant authorities.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office in Ottawa?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is based in Nashville, Tennessee, and has no office or staff in Ottawa or elsewhere in Canada. Engagements touching Ottawa are scoped and managed from Nashville, with licensed Ontario or Quebec investigators and the client's Canadian counsel engaged where local work or legal advice is needed.
